items.title: 12.3.2 Criterion for Existence of Limit of a Function

blocks.latex: \begin{gathered}\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \text{ if and only if} \\ \lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c^{+}} f(x) = L\end{gathered}
blocks.text_alt: limit of f of x as x tends to c equals L if and only if the left hand limit and the right hand limit at c are both equal to L

blocks.text: In words: the limit of \(f(x)\) at \(c\) exists and equals \(L\) exactly when the left hand limit and the right hand limit both exist and both equal \(L\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
"If and only if" works in both directions:
1. If both one-sided limits exist and are equal (to \(L\)), then \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\) exists and equals \(L\).
2. If \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L\), then both one-sided limits are \(L\).
So the limit does not exist when the two one-sided limits are different (the graph "jumps" at \(c\)), or when one of them does not exist.
Why this makes sense: a limit is one single number that \(f(x)\) approaches from every direction. If the left side heads for 3 and the right side heads for 4, there is no single number for \(f(x)\) to approach.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Method for a piecewise function at a joining point \(c\):
1. Find the left hand limit with the formula valid for \(x < c\).
2. Find the right hand limit with the formula valid for \(x > c\).
3. Compare: equal means the limit exists (and equals the common value); different means it does not exist.

blocks.title: Example 10
blocks.problem:
Determine whether \(\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)\) and \(\lim_{x \to 4} f(x)\) exist, when
\[f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + 1 & \text{if } 0 \le x \le 2 \\ 7 - x & \text{if } 2 < x < 4 \\ x & \text{if } 4 \le x \le 6 \end{cases}\]
steps:
Given: the three-piece function \(f\) above, defined for \(0 \le x \le 6\).
To find: whether \(\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)\) and \(\lim_{x \to 4} f(x)\) exist.
Method: \(x = 2\) and \(x = 4\) are the points where the formula changes, so we find the left hand and right hand limits at each point and use the criterion: the limit exists only if the two are equal.

(i) Step 1: Left hand limit at \(x = 2\)
For \(x\) close to 2 with \(x < 2\), \(f(x) = 2x + 1\).
\[\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 2^{-}} (2x + 1)\]
\[= 2(2) + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5\]
Why: on the left of 2 (\(0 \le x < 2\)) the first formula applies; \(2x + 1\) is a polynomial, so its limit is found by substitution.

(i) Step 2: Right hand limit at \(x = 2\)
For \(x\) close to 2 with \(x > 2\), \(f(x) = 7 - x\).
\[\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 2^{+}} (7 - x)\]
\[= 7 - 2 = 5\]
Why: on the right of 2 (\(2 < x < 4\)) the second formula applies.

(i) Step 3: Compare
\[\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 2^{+}} f(x) = 5\]
\[\Rightarrow \lim_{x \to 2} f(x) \text{ exists and } = 5\]
Why: by the criterion of 12.3.2, equal one-sided limits mean the limit exists and has the same value.

(ii) Step 4: Left hand limit at \(x = 4\)
For \(x\) close to 4 with \(x < 4\), \(f(x) = 7 - x\).
\[\lim_{x \to 4^{-}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 4^{-}} (7 - x)\]
\[= 7 - 4 = 3\]
Why: on the left of 4 (\(2 < x < 4\)) the second formula applies.

(ii) Step 5: Right hand limit at \(x = 4\)
For \(x\) close to 4 with \(x > 4\), \(f(x) = x\).
\[\lim_{x \to 4^{+}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 4^{+}} x = 4\]
Why: on the right of 4 (\(4 \le x \le 6\)) the third formula applies.

(ii) Step 6: Compare
\[\lim_{x \to 4^{-}} f(x) = 3\]
\[\lim_{x \to 4^{+}} f(x) = 4\]
\[3 \ne 4\]
Therefore \(\lim_{x \to 4} f(x)\) does not exist.
Why: the two sides approach different numbers, so there is no single limit; the graph jumps from height 3 to height 4 at \(x = 4\).

Check: take values very close to the points.
\[f(1.99) = 4.98,\quad f(2.01) = 4.99\]
Both are close to 5, as found.
\[f(3.99) = 3.01,\quad f(4.01) = 4.01\]
These stay near 3 on the left and near 4 on the right, so there is a jump at \(x = 4\).
blocks.answer: \(\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)\) exists and equals 5; \(\lim_{x \to 4} f(x)\) does not exist, because the left hand limit is 3 and the right hand limit is 4.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Notice that \(f(4) = 4\) is defined (third formula), yet \(\lim_{x \to 4} f(x)\) does not exist. The value of the function at a point and the limit at that point are different questions; in 12.3.3 continuity compares exactly these two.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L\) if and only if \(\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c^{+}} f(x) = L\).
2. Different one-sided limits: the limit does not exist.
3. For a piecewise function, check the limit at every point where the formula changes, using the correct piece on each side.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Stopping after one side: finding only \(\lim_{x \to 4^{-}} f(x) = 3\) and writing \(\lim_{x \to 4} f(x) = 3\).
2. Using the piece that contains the "=" sign for both sides: at \(x = 4\) the third piece (\(4 \le x\)) is for the right side only.
3. Concluding that the limit exists because \(f(c)\) is defined.
